analysis.one_liner: Lets disabled workers sue employee benefit plans in state court when the plan delays disability benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with no cosponsors, it sat in a House committee and subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1974 federal law, ERISA, generally blocks workers from suing their employer's benefit plan under state law. That means if a disability plan delays or drags out the benefits a worker paid for, the worker usually cannot recover damages for the harm the delay caused — only the benefits themselves. This bill would carve out an exception: disabled workers could bring state tort suits for damages arising from a plan's failure to pay disability benefits on time. The bill was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by employer disability plans whose benefits are delayed — people often already dealing with illness or injury and lost income. They would gain the ability to recover damages in state court for the harm a delayed payment caused, not just the delayed benefits. State courts and trial lawyers handling such suits would also see more work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA's preemption section so that state tort claims for damages from a disability plan's failure to timely provide benefits are not blocked by federal law.

Currently, a worker whose disability benefits are delayed generally cannot get damages for the resulting harm under state law; the bill would change that, giving plans a financial reason to pay on time.
The change would apply to plan failures occurring after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Disability insurers and employers that sponsor self-funded benefit plans, which would face new exposure to state-court damages suits over delayed benefit decisions. Some of that cost could be passed to plan participants through premiums or reduced benefits.

drawbacks.text: Employers and insurers have long argued that ERISA's uniform federal rules keep benefit plans affordable and predictable; exposing plans to state juries and punitive-style damages could raise costs, and plans might pass those costs on to workers through higher premiums or lower benefits.
The bill was a narrow, one-clause fix with no cosponsors and no hearing record, so there is no evidence in the record about how much litigation it would generate or how courts would apply it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For disabled workers stuck waiting for benefits they contracted for, the potential gain is real: the threat of damages is the main lever to make plans pay promptly. The cost falls on insurers and plan sponsors, and some of it may trickle to workers as premiums. The bill is a narrow tool rather than a full fix — it covers disability plans only, and only failures occurring after enactment — but its core trade-off favors workers over plan administrators.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee, and then sent to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on March 20, 2001.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On May 30, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations — the last action of its two-year life.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Disability insurers and employer-sponsored benefit plans are better off, because they remain shielded by ERISA preemption from state-court damages suits over delayed disability benefits. Workers whose benefits are delayed continue to have no state-law remedy for the harm the delay causes.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleagues cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died there.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled the committee calendar; no action was taken on the bill at any point in the 107th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote, so no party breakdown exists; it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and sat in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Disability insurers and employer-sponsored benefit plans
industries.note: The bill would have exposed plans to state-court damages suits when they delay disability benefits, a cost they avoid today under ERISA preemption. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against workers who wait for benefits they were promised.
A new category of state tort suits over delayed disability benefits would create legal work, and in this bill the lawyers' interest runs alongside the workers the suits would serve.
